newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan launches most powerful radio telescope.
newsitem.headline: Japan launches most powerful radio telescope.

text.p: Japan on Wednesday launched a satellite radio telescope capable of seeing objects in space equivalent to a grain of rice on earth.

Described as one million times more powerful than the United States' Hubble telescope in scientific terms, the telescope will link up with ground-based radio telescopes to probe major sources in the galaxy, such as quasars and black holes.

A statement by the Education Ministry's Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS), which is in charge of the project, said the satellite, which uses radio astronomy technology, had a life expectancy of three to five years.

It said the 830 kg (1,830 lb) Muses-B satellite radio telescope was sent into orbit on the world's largest solid-fuel rocket, the M-5, a Japan-developed rocket. The launch was from a site in the town of Uchinoura, southwest Japan.
The rocket was designed to meet increasing demands for larger payloads and is powerful enough for missions to Mars, Venus and outlying asteroids.
Future missions for the rocket include a flight to the moon and a probe that will orbit Mars to observe the red planet's geomagnetic field.
The statement said the satellite's magnifying power for celestial bodies was equivalent to being able to see from Tokyo a grain of rice in Sydney.
The satellite is part of an international project.
Among foreign institutes involved are the National Radio Astronomy Observatory of the United States, the European VLBI Network and the Australia Telescope National Facility.
Professor Hisashi Hirabayashi of the ISAS told Reuters the new radio telescope was not optical like Hubble, but was able to see images much more distant in space.
"It is 1,000 times more powerful than Hubble in terms of one-dimensional image, but in two-dimensional terms, it is a million times stronger," he said.

"In terms of resolution, it is going to be the world's most powerful. If the Hubble telescope can detect a single point, our telescope would be able to differentiate a million segments of a (radio) image of that same size."
